primary_category.subcategory: A2.4 Information search, retrieval, gathering, and evaluation

evidence.quote: I had the standard checklist, the verbal mention from turnover about the new valve, and technically the work order attachment was available if I'd gone looking for it.
evidence.explanation: The task centers on gathering and verifying information from multiple sources (checklist, verbal turnover, work order) to confirm equipment configuration.

evidence.quote: I did not pull the fifteen-minute trend from the plant computer, even though it was right there available.
evidence.explanation: The episode is defined by whether the operator retrieves and evaluates available diagnostic data before forming a conclusion.

evidence.quote: The temperature drift was smaller and only visible if you were looking right at the local gauge, and the odor was faint enough that I almost second-guessed whether I was smelling anything at all.
evidence.explanation: The operator gathers and compares multiple perceptual and instrument-based information sources to decide what to report.

secondary_categories.subcategory: A2.1 Uncodified visual or auditory information processing

evidence.location: Timeline, rounds near the pump coupling
evidence.quote: I heard a pretty loud, intermittent knocking sound. That got my attention immediately, it's the kind of noise that makes you stop.
evidence.explanation: The operator interprets an auditory anomaly signal that is not reducible to a fixed rule, requiring perceptual pattern recognition of an abnormal mechanical condition.

evidence.quote: My first thought honestly went back to the week before — we'd had a similar RTD on another pump throw a high reading that turned out to be a wiring fault... So I figured this was probably the same kind of thing.
evidence.explanation: The operator forms a diagnostic explanation by generalizing from a prior case to the present instrument reading, an act of abstraction and inference beyond raw data retrieval.

evidence.quote: I had a partial picture — noise that turned out later to be a loose coupling guard, a temperature that had crept up some more, and that odor still there... I put together what I had, decided it was workable, and kept the train running to finish the test on schedule.
evidence.explanation: The operator synthesizes multiple incomplete evidence streams under time and coordination constraints to reach a non-routine go/no-go judgment, weighing dependencies (deadline, advisor availability, coordination cost) rather than following a scripted next step.

evidence.quote: I started working through it the way I always do, valve by valve, left side first, then across to the discharge header.
evidence.explanation: Manual verification and operation of valves and pump controls implies coordinated hand-operated manipulation of physical equipment, though the interview does not describe fine motor detail explicitly.

evidence.quote: A little later, doing my rounds near the pump coupling, I heard a pretty loud, intermittent knocking sound.
evidence.explanation: The operator physically moves through the pump room and plant spaces to perform lineup verification and rounds, maintaining spatial orientation across equipment locations.

evidence.quote: Swapping trains meant coordination, paperwork, and possibly missing the window entirely. The Shift Technical Advisor was tied up on another issue.
evidence.explanation: The operator must weigh coordination dependencies with other personnel and organizational processes in reaching the final decision, though this is peripheral to the operator's own primary task.

evidence.quote: I put together what I had, decided it was workable, and kept the train running to finish the test on schedule.
evidence.explanation: The operator makes the final continue-versus-trip call independently in the field, without the Shift Technical Advisor's direct involvement, indicating meaningful discretion over the operational decision, though within a proceduralized surveillance framework.

evidence.quote: Found out afterward, when control room called down, that it wasn't lined up the way the updated paperwork called for.
evidence.explanation: The operator's work is checked against updated paperwork and reviewed by the control room, showing an external verification layer, though not continuous direct supervision.

evidence.quote: The Shift Technical Advisor was tied up on another issue... control room called down.

evidence.quote: I got to the pump room after grabbing the surveillance procedure and the routine lineup checklist.

evidence.quote: On startup, the bearing temperature RTD came up slightly above the normal band, not alarming, but above where I usually see it.
evidence.explanation: Conditions were mostly within an anticipated procedural framework but included several unplanned deviations (added valve, elevated RTD, knocking, odor) that reduced predictability of inputs during the shift.

evidence.quote: I heard a pretty loud, intermittent knocking sound... We had maybe under thirty minutes left in the window.
evidence.explanation: The operator must respond to multiple unplanned anomalies (valve discrepancy, abnormal temperature, noise, odor) and integrate them into a real-time decision under deadline pressure, beyond the scope of the routine procedure.

task_anchors.task_description: Verifying a pump train valve lineup against a standard checklist while a recently added isolation valve required cross-checking against a work order attachment.
Interpreting a slightly elevated bearing temperature reading using memory of a prior similar event rather than pulling current trend data.
Detecting and prioritizing among simultaneous auditory, thermal, and olfactory cues during equipment rounds and reporting to the control room.
Integrating partial diagnostic evidence under a closing surveillance deadline to decide whether to continue running the pump train or trip and swap trains.

evidence: I had the standard checklist, the verbal mention from turnover about the new valve, and technically the work order attachment was available if I'd gone looking for it.
I did not pull the fifteen-minute trend from the plant computer, even though it was right there available.
The noise was what stood out, so that's what I focused on and what I called up to the control room about.

Swapping trains meant coordination, paperwork, and possibly missing the window entirely. The Shift Technical Advisor was tied up on another issue. I put together what I had, decided it was workable, and kept the train running.
